questions.q: A converging lens has a focal length of 0.25 m. What is its power?
questions.solution: Power is one divided by the focal length in metres: \(P = \frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{0.25}\) = 4.0 D. A converging lens has a positive power.

questions.q: Which lens corrects short sight (myopia), and why?

options.A: A diverging lens, because the eye focuses distant objects in front of the retina.
options.B: A converging lens, because the eye focuses distant objects in front of the retina.
options.C: A diverging lens, because the eye focuses near objects behind the retina.
options.D: A cylindrical lens, because the cornea is unevenly curved.

questions.solution: A short-sighted eye is too powerful, or too long: light from distant objects comes to a focus in front of the retina. A diverging lens spreads the light slightly first, so the eye then focuses it on the retina. Cylindrical lenses correct astigmatism.

questions.q: Which cells in the retina allow us to see colour?

options.D: Neither: colour is detected by the lens

questions.solution: Cones come in three types, most sensitive to red, green and blue light, and give colour vision in bright light. They are packed most closely at the fovea. Rods work in dim light but cannot tell colours apart.

questions.q: A sound has an intensity of \(1.0 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{W m}^{-2}\). The threshold of hearing is \(1.0 \times 10^{-12}\ \text{W m}^{-2}\). What is the intensity level of the sound?
questions.solution: Intensity level = \(10\log\left(\frac{I}{I_{0}}\right)\). The ratio of the intensities is a million, whose logarithm is 6, so the level is 10 × 6 = 60 dB. Leaving out the factor of ten (6 dB) gives the level in bels.

questions.q: The graph shows an equal loudness curve for the human ear. At about what frequency is the ear most sensitive?

figure.alt: Intensity level against frequency on a logarithmic scale. The curve is high at low frequencies, falls to a minimum between 1 kilohertz and 10 kilohertz, and rises again at high frequencies.

questions.solution: The curve shows the intensity level needed for a sound to seem equally loud at each frequency. Where the curve is lowest, the least intensity is needed, so the ear is most sensitive there: at about 3 kHz, where the ear canal resonates. A frequency of 30 kHz is above the range of human hearing altogether.

questions.q: The graph shows a normal ECG trace for one heartbeat. What does the QRS wave show?

figure.alt: Potential difference against time for one heartbeat: a small rounded wave labelled P, then a tall, sharp wave labelled QRS, then a rounded wave labelled T.

questions.solution: The P wave is the depolarisation and contraction of the atria. The large QRS wave is the depolarisation and contraction of the ventricles. The T wave is the repolarisation and relaxation of the ventricles.

questions.q: Soft tissue has a density of \(1060\ \text{kg m}^{-3}\), and ultrasound travels through it at \(1540\ \text{m s}^{-1}\). What is its acoustic impedance?
questions.solution: Acoustic impedance is density times the speed of sound: \(Z = \rho c = 1060 \times 1540 = 1.6 \times 10^{6}\ \text{kg m}^{-2}\ \text{s}^{-1}\).

questions.q: Why is a gel put between an ultrasound transducer and the patient's skin?

options.A: To remove the air gap, so that most of the ultrasound enters the body and is not reflected.
options.C: To increase the frequency of the ultrasound.
options.D: To make the ultrasound travel faster.

questions.solution: Air has a very different acoustic impedance from skin, so almost all the ultrasound would be reflected at an air gap. The coupling gel has an impedance close to that of skin, so nearly all of it is transmitted.

questions.q: How does a piezoelectric transducer produce ultrasound?

options.B: An alternating potential difference across the crystal makes it vibrate.
options.C: A magnet moves inside a coil.

questions.solution: A piezoelectric crystal changes shape when a potential difference is applied across it. An alternating potential difference at the right frequency makes it vibrate and send out ultrasound. The effect also works in reverse, so the same crystal detects the returning echoes.

questions.q: In an endoscope, why must the bundle of optical fibres that carries the image be coherent?

options.A: So that the fibres stay in the same positions relative to each other at both ends, keeping the image in order.
options.B: So that the light in every fibre has the same wavelength.
options.C: So that more light reaches the area being viewed.
options.D: So that the bundle can bend more easily.

questions.solution: In a coherent bundle each fibre is in the same relative position at both ends, so each carries one small part of the image to the right place. The bundle that only carries light down to illuminate the area can be incoherent, which is cheaper.

questions.q: Which nuclei in the body does a magnetic resonance (MR) scanner mainly detect?
questions.solution: An MR scanner uses a strong magnetic field and pulses of radio waves to make hydrogen nuclei (protons) absorb and then re-emit radio-frequency signals. The body is rich in hydrogen, in water and fat. The method uses no ionising radiation.

questions.q: X-rays pass through 2.0 cm of a material with a linear attenuation coefficient of \(0.50\ \text{cm}^{-1}\). What percentage of the original intensity gets through?
questions.solution: \(I = I_{0}e^{-\mu x}\), and \(\mu x = 0.50 \times 2.0 = 1.0\). The fraction transmitted is \(e^{-1.0}\) = 0.37, which is 37%.

questions.q: A material has a linear attenuation coefficient of \(0.20\ \text{mm}^{-1}\) for X-rays. What is its half-value thickness?
questions.solution: The half-value thickness is the thickness that halves the intensity: \(x_{\frac{1}{2}} = \frac{\ln 2}{\mu} = \frac{0.693}{0.20}\) = 3.5 mm. Leaving out \(\ln 2\) (5.0 mm) is the usual slip.

questions.q: A radioactive tracer has a physical half-life of 6.0 hours and a biological half-life of 3.0 hours. What is its effective half-life in the body?
questions.solution: \(\frac{1}{T_{E}} = \frac{1}{T_{B}} + \frac{1}{T_{P}} = \frac{1}{3.0} + \frac{1}{6.0} = \frac{1}{2.0}\), so the effective half-life = 2.0 hours. It is always shorter than either half-life alone, because both processes remove the tracer.

questions.q: Why is technetium-99m well suited for use as a medical tracer?

options.A: It emits alpha particles, which are easy to detect outside the body.
options.B: It has a half-life of many years, so it can be stored.
options.C: It emits only gamma rays and has a half-life of a few hours.

questions.solution: Gamma rays pass out of the body to a gamma camera and do little damage on the way; alpha or beta particles would be absorbed in tissue and cause harm. A half-life of about six hours is long enough for the scan but short enough that the dose soon falls.

questions.q: Why is a patient given a barium meal before an X-ray of the stomach?

options.A: Barium is radioactive and emits X-rays.
options.B: Barium protects the stomach from the X-rays.
options.C: Barium makes the X-rays more energetic.
options.D: Barium absorbs X-rays strongly, so the stomach shows up against the surrounding soft tissue.

questions.solution: Soft tissues all absorb X-rays to a similar, small extent, so they give little contrast. Barium has a high proton number and absorbs X-rays strongly. Lining the stomach with it makes the stomach's outline stand out. It is a contrast medium.
